chapter.name: The State, the Government, and You

questions.q: The chapter lists four important parts of a state. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
questions.a: A national language is not one of the four parts; the four parts are people, land (a fixed territory), government and sovereignty.

questions.q: Which statement best explains what sovereignty means for a state?
o: The state has complete control over its own matters, and no other state or outside body can interfere in its internal affairs
The state has a large army that is stronger than the armies of its neighbours
The state has a permanent population whose families have lived there for many years
The state has boundaries made by natural features such as rivers and mountains
questions.a: Sovereignty is complete control over its own matters: the state makes and implements laws for its own needs and no outside state or body can interfere in its internal affairs.

questions.q: Match each part of a state in Column A with its meaning in Column B. Column A: 1. People 2. Land 3. Government 4. Sovereignty. Column B: P. A system to run the country Q. The citizens who live in the country R. Full power to make laws and take decisions without any outside control S. A fixed area or territory
questions.a: 1-Q, 2-S, 3-P, 4-R: people are the citizens, land is the fixed territory, government is the system that runs the country and sovereignty is full power without outside control.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Sovereignty is an essential feature of a state. Reason (R): A permanent population develops its own culture and society, which identifies with the territory where it lives.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both are true, but R does not explain A. Sovereignty is essential because it lets the state control its own matters and make and implement its own laws with no outside interference; R is about the permanent population, a different feature.

questions.q: True or False: After an election a new government may come to power, but the state remains the same. Give the verdict and one reason.
questions.a: True. The government is only one part of the state and can change after elections, while the state with its people, land and sovereignty continues.
s: States the verdict: True
Reason: the government is only one part of the state; it changes but the state remains

questions.q: (a) What is a government, according to the chapter? (b) Name the three things its leaders, ministers and officials do.
questions.a: (a) A group of people or a system that runs the country, including leaders, ministers and officials. (b) They make laws, enforce laws and resolve disputes.
s: (a) A group of people or a system that runs the country
(b) Make laws, enforce laws and resolve disputes

questions.q: Ice Island research base covers an area whose boundary line is agreed with the two neighbouring countries. A station council makes rules, enforces them and settles quarrels, and no outside country or body can interfere in its affairs. 120 scientists work there; each stays six months and then returns home, and none has lived there for more than a year. Priya says, 'The base already has three of the four parts of a state, so with a few more scientists it would become a full state.' (a) Which three parts of a state does the base have? (b) Which part is missing, and why? (c) Is Priya right? Give your verdict.
questions.a: (a) A defined territory (a boundary agreed with neighbours), a government (the council makes and enforces rules and settles quarrels) and sovereignty (no outside interference). (b) A permanent population: the scientists come for a while and move on, like tourists; they do not usually live there or identify with the place, so they do not form a shared society of their own. (c) Priya's conclusion is wrong. Accept 'No' or 'Partly right' with the reason: three parts are present, but more short-stay scientists are still not a permanent population; people who usually live there and identify with the place are needed, and a state needs all four parts.
s: (a) Names territory, government and sovereignty from the data
(b) Permanent population missing: scientists only stay a while and leave, with no identification with the place
(c) 'No' or 'Partly right', with the reason that more short-stay people still do not make a permanent population

questions.q: Answer each part about the state and the government. (a) Define a state. (b) Name the four parts of a state. (c) Which of the four parts can change after an election? (d) Give the chapter's comparison of the state with a school. (e) Give one reason why people use the words 'state' and 'government' as if they mean the same thing.
questions.a: (a) A state is a political organisation that has the authority to govern a defined territory and its population. (b) People, land (territory), government and sovereignty. (c) The government. (d) The state is like a school and the government like the principal and teachers: teachers come and go but the school remains. (e) The government runs the daily work of the state, and we usually interact with the government, not the whole state.
s: (a) Political organisation with authority to govern a defined territory and its population
(b) People, land, government, sovereignty
(c) The government
(d) State = school, government = principal and teachers who come and go
(e) Government runs daily work of the state / we interact with the government

questions.q: Read the passage and answer the questions. Kavya studies the newspapers of Varunia, an imaginary country, for one week. She finds 40 headlines that use the word 'government' or 'state'. 26 say 'the government ...' and 14 say 'the state ...'. Of the 14 'state' headlines, 10 report a decision taken by a minister or a government department, such as a new bus route or new school timings. The other 4 say: 'The state's border with its neighbour, agreed in 1950, has not changed'; 'The state's border posts are being repainted'; 'No outside country can interfere in the state's internal affairs'; and 'The state's permanent population has crossed 8 crore'. (a) What percentage of the 'state' headlines report the work of the government? Give the answer to the nearest whole number. (b) Which parts of a state do the other 4 headlines point to? (c) Give one reason from the chapter why the writers of the 10 headlines used the word 'state' for the government's work. (d) Kavya concludes, 'Most state headlines are really about the government, so the two words mean the same thing.' Judge her conclusion using the data.
questions.a: (a) 10 out of 14 = 71.4%, about 71%. (b) Land (a defined territory with agreed boundaries), sovereignty (no outside interference) and people (a permanent population). (c) The government acts on behalf of the state and is the face of the state we see every day; it runs the daily work of the state, and we usually interact with the government, not the whole state. (d) Her conclusion is wrong (accept 'partly right' if the reason is given). The data show why the words are mixed up, since about 71% of the 'state' headlines are really about the government. But the other 4 headlines (about 29%) are about territory, sovereignty and the people, parts of the state that are not the government. The government is only one part of the state, so the words differ in meaning.
s: (b) Land or territory, sovereignty and people (permanent population)
(c) Government acts on behalf of the state / runs its daily work / is the part we interact with
(d) Judgement: the words still differ; 4 headlines are about other parts of the state, and the government is only one part

questions.q: According to the chapter, the police in India are part of which level of government?
questions.a: The state government: the police maintain law and order within each state and are part of the state government.

questions.q: A police team in a town runs a programme in which students learn to wear helmets and follow traffic signals. How does the chapter describe this kind of work?
o: Work beyond crime control that promotes safety and a better quality of life
Work of the judiciary, because it teaches people about the law
Work of the legislature, because it creates new traffic rules
Work that the police are not allowed to do because no crime has taken place
questions.a: It is police work beyond crime control: awareness programmes on road safety are part of how the police promote safety and a better quality of life.

questions.q: The Karnataka legislature passes a law that shops near schools may not sell tobacco. According to the chapter, which statement describes what happens to this law next?
o: A government department carries out the law, and the judiciary ensures that it is followed
The legislature itself inspects every shop near a school, and the department decides any disputes
The judiciary carries out the law in every town, and the department ensures that it is followed
The police rewrite the law separately for each town, and the courts then announce it to the shops
questions.a: A government department carries out the law and the judiciary ensures it is followed: departments, part of the executive, implement the policies and laws made by the legislature, and the judiciary ensures these laws are followed.

questions.q: Read the statements. I. The police are agents of the state who can legally use force to keep people safe. II. The police work closely with courts and prisons. III. In every country the legislature, executive and judiciary are completely separate from one another. Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and II only are correct; III is wrong because in some countries the legislature, executive and judiciary are separate, while in others they may overlap.

questions.q: Name any two topics on which, according to the chapter, the police run awareness programmes.
questions.a: Any two of: road safety, drug abuse, women's safety.
s: First correct topic (road safety / drug abuse / women's safety)
Second correct topic

questions.q: Residents of a town in Gujarat are unhappy with the people who make their state's laws. Use the chapter's diagram of people, police and the organs of government. (a) Through which link in the diagram can the residents change who represents them? (b) Which organ of government do these representatives sit in, and what is its job?
questions.a: (a) The people elect leaders to represent them, so at the next election the residents can vote for different representatives. (b) The legislature, which makes the laws.
s: (a) People elect leaders to represent them: vote for different representatives
(b) The legislature, which makes laws

questions.q: Divya notices that police officers in Chennai and in Patna do the same kind of work. She says, 'So the police everywhere in India must be run by the Union Government in Delhi.' Check her claim: (a) which level of government are the police part of, according to the chapter? (b) Where is each police force responsible for law and order, and with whom does it work directly? (c) Is Divya right? Explain.
questions.a: (a) The police are part of the state government. (b) They are responsible for law and order within each state and work directly with local communities in towns, cities and villages. (c) No. Doing similar work does not mean the same government runs them: the Chennai police belong to the Tamil Nadu government and the Patna police to the Bihar government.
s: (a) Part of the state government
(b) Law and order within each state; work directly with local communities
(c) No: similar work, but each force belongs to its own state government

questions.q: Answer these parts about the police and the organs of government. (a) Who maintains law and order within each state in India? (b) A police officer hands the file of a robbery case to a magistrate's court. Which part of the criminal justice system is the officer working with? (c) Which organ of government makes the laws that government departments implement? (d) Which organ of government do we interact with most in daily life?
questions.a: (a) The police. (b) The courts (the judiciary). (c) The legislature. (d) The executive, through its various departments.
s: (a) The police
(b) The courts / judiciary
(c) The legislature
(d) The executive

questions.q: Read the passage and answer the questions. A local newspaper in Hubballi reports one week. On Monday, police officers investigated a chain-snatching, caught the culprit and prepared the case. On Wednesday, residents of a colony complained that tap water had come on only 2 days out of 7. On Friday, a few of these residents stood quietly outside the municipal water office holding placards. The police stood by and kept the road open, and the water department's engineer came out, heard them and promised a new pipeline. (a) To which organ of government will the police present Monday's case? (b) Which pillar of government does the water department belong to, and what is the job of such departments? (c) Name one right protected by the Constitution that the residents used with their placards. (d) A reader writes, 'The police should have sent the residents home and settled the water problem themselves.' Do you agree? Use what the chapter says about the police and about government departments.
questions.a: (a) The judiciary (the courts). (b) The executive: its departments implement the policies and laws made by the legislature, and they are the part of government we meet most in daily life. (c) Freedom of speech. (d) No. The police keep law and order, but they must respect the rights guaranteed under the Constitution, and the residents were peaceful. Supplying water is the work of the water department, a part of the executive, so the residents were right to take the problem there, and the engineer was the right person to answer them.
s: (a) The judiciary / courts
(b) Executive: departments implement policies and laws made by the legislature
(c) Freedom of speech
(d) No: police must respect rights of peaceful people, and water supply is the department's job

questions.q: The word 'democracy' comes from two Greek words, demos and kratos. What does it mean?
o: Rule by a few rich families
questions.a: Rule by the people: demos means people and kratos means rule.

questions.q: Country M elects its president every five years in free and fair elections, but once elected the president may change any law and is not bound by any constitution. Country N's elected president must act within limits set by its constitution. Which statement follows the chapter?
o: Only N fully fits the idea of a republic, as a republic also limits rulers' power through a constitution or laws
Both M and N are full republics, because in both countries the head of state is elected and does not inherit the post
Neither M nor N is a republic, because a republic's head of state must always be chosen by elected representatives
Only M is a full republic, because its people have freely chosen to give their elected president full power to act
questions.a: Only N fully fits: in a republic the head of state is elected and not hereditary, and there are also limits on the power of rulers through a constitution or laws, which M does not have.

questions.q: Read the statements. I. Canada is a democracy but not a republic, because it has a monarch. II. In a republic, the rule of law is more powerful than the wishes of the majority. III. India's Constitution allows a representative majority to take away a citizen's fundamental rights. Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and II only are correct. Canada has a monarch, so it is a democracy but not a republic, and in a republic the rule of law is more powerful than the wishes of the majority. III is wrong: constitutional provisions and the law ensure that rule by a representative majority does not violate the fundamental rights of any citizen.

questions.q: Assertion (A): India is a republic. Reason (R): India's head of state, the president, is elected and does not inherit the post.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: in a republic the head of state is elected (directly or indirectly) and not hereditary, as India's president is.

questions.q: True or False: Every democracy is a republic. Give the verdict and a reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Not all democracies are republics: the UK, Canada and Sweden are democracies, but each has a monarch who inherits the post, so they are not republics.
s: States the verdict: False
Reason: some democracies, such as the UK, Canada or Sweden, have a monarch and so are not republics

questions.q: A company wants to lease hill land that belongs to a tribal community to build a resort. Most people in the nearby town support the plan because it would bring jobs, but the community refuses. (a) According to the chapter, what does the company need before it can lease this land? (b) Which idea about a republic does this protection show?
questions.a: (a) The permission of the local community and due legal process; such lands are protected by law for the community's use. (b) The rule of law protects the rights of a smaller group even when a larger number of people want something else; this guards against the dominance of the majority.
s: (a) Permission of the local community and due legal process
(b) Law protects the rights of the smaller group against the wishes of the majority

questions.q: Answer briefly. (a) Name two countries that the chapter gives as examples of both a democracy and a republic. (b) Name one country that is a democracy but not a republic. (c) Which tribe's sacred hills in Odisha were protected when mining was not allowed?
questions.a: (a) India and the U.S.A. (b) Any one of the UK, Canada or Sweden. (c) The Dongria Kondh.
s: (a) India and the U.S.A.
(b) UK / Canada / Sweden
(c) Dongria Kondh

questions.q: A draft constitution for an imaginary country, Ruvania, has four clauses. Clause 1: Every adult votes in free and fair elections to parliament every five years. Clause 2: The head of state is the eldest child of the previous king or queen. Clause 3: No law limits the powers of the head of state. Clause 4: All citizens have equal rights that no law passed by a majority may take away. (a) Which clause makes Ruvania a democracy, and why? (b) Which two clauses stop it from being a republic? Explain. (c) Which clause guards against the dominance of the majority? (d) Suggest how the clauses that stop Ruvania from being a republic should be changed to make it a democratic republic like India. (e) A student says, 'Clause 1 alone makes Ruvania just like India.' Give your judgement.
questions.a: (a) Clause 1: in a democracy the people choose their government through free and fair elections. (b) Clause 2, because in a republic the head of state is elected, not hereditary; and Clause 3, because a republic sets limits on the power of rulers through a constitution or laws. (c) Clause 4, which stops a majority from taking away the rights of smaller groups. (d) Let the head of state be elected, directly or indirectly (India's president is elected by elected representatives), and add limits on the head of state's powers in the constitution. (e) The student is wrong. Clause 1 makes Ruvania a democracy, but with a hereditary head of unlimited power it would be like the UK, Canada or Sweden, democracies with a monarch, and worse, since its ruler's powers have no limits. India is both a democracy and a republic, with an elected head of state and limits set by the Constitution.
s: (a) Clause 1: free and fair elections
(b) Clauses 2 and 3: hereditary head; no limits on power
(c) Clause 4 protects against dominance of the majority
(d) Elected head of state (directly or indirectly) and limits on power in the constitution
(e) Judgement: wrong; elections alone make a democracy, India is also a republic

questions.q: Read the passage and answer the questions. In a civics class in Kochi, Ms Thomas shows the class the Preamble to the Constitution, which uses the words 'democratic' and 'republic' together. She explains: 'The government can use force to maintain law and order, but the Constitution limits its powers. Otherwise, elected members and government officers might use their power unchecked, which would threaten citizens' rights. Elected leaders cannot pass laws that go against people's basic rights, like freedom of speech, religion, or equality before the law.' (a) Which two words does the Preamble use together? (b) According to Ms Thomas, what limits the powers of the government? (c) Name any two basic rights that elected leaders cannot pass laws against. (d) A party with a large majority plans a law to stop one religious group from praying in public. Using the passage, can it pass such a law? Why?
questions.a: (a) 'Democratic' and 'republic'. (b) The Constitution. (c) Any two of freedom of speech, freedom of religion and equality before the law. (d) No. Freedom of religion is a basic right, and elected leaders cannot pass laws that go against basic rights, however large their majority, because the Constitution limits their power.
s: (a) Democratic and republic
(b) The Constitution
(c) Two of speech, religion, equality before the law
(d) No: freedom of religion is a basic right the Constitution protects from any majority

questions.q: Which organ of government makes laws for the country?
questions.a: The legislature is the lawmaking body that makes laws for the country.

questions.q: Officers of the permanent executive are selected through examinations conducted by which body?
questions.a: The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) conducts the examinations through which permanent executive officers are selected.

questions.q: Match each person in Column A with the part of government in Column B. Column A: 1. A member of a state Vidhan Sabha who votes on a new law 2. A chief minister 3. An IAS officer in charge of a district 4. A governor of a state. Column B: P. Permanent executive Q. Legislature R. Political executive with a mostly formal role S. Political executive that makes big decisions
questions.a: 1-Q, 2-S, 3-P, 4-R: the Vidhan Sabha member is in the legislature, the chief minister is the political executive making big decisions, the IAS officer is permanent executive and the governor is political executive with a mostly formal role.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The power of the political executive depends on the trust and support of the people. Reason (R): Officers of the political executive are selected through examinations and stay in office after every election.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: A is true but R is false: the political executive is elected by the people for a fixed time, usually five years; it is the permanent executive that is selected by examinations and stays after elections.

questions.q: (a) What are the two parts of the executive? (b) Give one other name for officers of the permanent executive.
questions.a: (a) The political executive and the permanent executive. (b) Bureaucrats or civil servants.
s: (a) Political executive and permanent executive
(b) Bureaucrats / civil servants

questions.q: True or False: C.B. Muthamma was the first woman to join the Indian Administrative Service. Give the verdict and correct the statement if needed.
questions.a: False. C.B. Muthamma was the first woman to join the Indian Foreign Service, in 1949.
s: States the verdict: False
Correction: she was the first woman to join the Indian Foreign Service (1949)

questions.q: Rohan reads the Constitution of India and finds no article that uses the words 'political executive' or 'permanent executive'. He says, 'So this division of the executive into two parts is just made up by textbook writers.' (a) What does the chapter say about whether the Constitution defines these two terms? (b) Where, according to the chapter, does the distinction come from? (c) Is Rohan right? Give your verdict.
questions.a: (a) The Constitution of India does not explicitly define the 'political executive' and the 'permanent executive'. (b) The distinction is an inherent part of India's parliamentary system, derived from constitutional principles and governance conventions. (c) Partly right: he is right that the Constitution does not explicitly define the two terms, but wrong that the division is made up, because it comes from constitutional principles and the way governance has worked.
s: (a) The Constitution does not explicitly define the two terms
(b) Inherent in the parliamentary system, from constitutional principles and governance conventions
(c) Partly right: no explicit definition, but the distinction is real

questions.q: Here are three news items from one week. Item 1: The Prime Minister meets leaders in Japan on behalf of India. Item 2: The Union ministers set a goal that every village will have piped water within five years. Item 3: District officers in Bihar keep a record of every village connected to piped water and of each decision taken. (a) Which part of the executive acts in Item 1, and which of its jobs does this show? (b) Which job of the same part does Item 2 show? (c) Which part of the executive acts in Item 3, and which function of the bureaucracy does it show? (d) In which of the three items does the power of those acting depend on the trust and support of the people? Why?
questions.a: (a) The political executive: representing India in other countries. (b) Setting goals for the country (making big decisions). (c) The permanent executive (bureaucracy): record-keeping of government work, decisions and procedures. (d) Items 1 and 2, because the Prime Minister and the Union ministers are elected leaders of the political executive, whose power depends on the trust and support of the people; the district officers in Item 3 are selected through examinations, not elected.
s: (a) Political executive: representing India in other countries
(b) Setting goals / making big decisions
(c) Permanent executive: record-keeping
(d) Items 1 and 2: elected leaders whose power depends on the people's trust

questions.q: Read the passage and answer the questions. A Class 7 group from Ranchi visits the Jharkhand Vidhan Sabha, which has 81 members. The guide says that last week a bill on safe school buses, introduced by the state's ministers, was passed by 52 votes to 29, and that the new law now applies to every school in Jharkhand. At the gate the students see a large portrait of the Governor of Jharkhand. (a) What percentage of the members voted for the bill? Give the answer to the nearest whole number. (b) Will this law also apply to schools in Odisha? Give the chapter's reason. (c) Sunil says, 'The Governor's portrait is at the gate, so the Governor must be the one who takes the big decisions in Jharkhand.' What does the chapter say about the Governor's role? (d) The 29 members who voted against the bill ask that the law should not apply to schools in their own areas. Should their request be accepted? Justify using the data and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 52 out of 81 = 64.2%, about 64%. (b) No. The states have their own legislatures, which make laws only for the state, so a Jharkhand law does not apply in Odisha. (c) The Governor belongs to the political executive but mostly has a formal or symbolic role; the big decisions are taken by the Chief Minister and the ministers. (d) No. The bill was passed by 52 votes to 29, so it is a law of the state, and the legislature creates rules that apply to everyone. Governance happens through well-defined laws, not personal wishes or arbitrary decisions, so the law applies to every school in Jharkhand, including those in the areas of members who voted against it.
s: (b) No: a state legislature makes laws only for its own state
(c) Governor's role is mostly formal or symbolic; big decisions by the Chief Minister and ministers
(d) No: passed 52 to 29, the law applies to everyone; governance by well-defined laws, not personal wishes

questions.q: Under which Act can a citizen ask a government office how much money was spent on building roads in her neighbourhood?
o: The Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act
questions.a: The Right to Information (RTI) Act, through which we can ask for information about government actions of public interest.

questions.q: The government builds schools and hires teachers so that education is free for children. Which of the government's three roles does this show?
questions.a: Provider: the government provides public welfare and infrastructure, such as free education through schools and teachers.

questions.q: Before Diwali, government food-safety officers in Lucknow test sweets from 120 shops and stop the sale of 9 batches found unsafe. According to the chapter, which of the government's three roles does this mainly show?
questions.a: Regulator: the chapter gives initiatives to ensure food safety as an example of the government regulating economic activity; protector refers to law and defence, and provider to public welfare and infrastructure.

questions.q: True or False: In Bagepalli, near Bengaluru, information obtained through an RTI request helped citizens get poorly done roadwork completed properly. Give the verdict and one line of reason.
questions.a: True. A local citizen filed an RTI to learn the money allocated for the roadwork; with this information a group of citizens confronted the officials, who then had the work completed to everyone's satisfaction.
s: States the verdict: True
Reason: the RTI gave the money allocated, citizens confronted the officials and the work was completed

questions.q: Answer briefly. (a) Name the national online portal on which a person can lodge a complaint against a government department. (b) Which bodies does the government have to investigate matters of corruption? (c) How does voting in elections help a citizen get her issues addressed?
questions.a: (a) The Public Grievances Portal. (b) Vigilance commissions. (c) By voting, she helps elect the leaders who care most about the issues she cares about and have the best plans for them.
s: (a) Public Grievances Portal
(b) Vigilance commissions
(c) Voting helps elect leaders who care about her issues and have the best plans

questions.q: Pooja says, 'India has a Constitution, thousands of laws, elected representatives and a vast bureaucracy, so there can be no problems such as bribery or poor roads in our country.' Check her claim using the chapter.
questions.a: Her claim is wrong. The chapter says that, although these help us greatly, the country still faces problems such as bribery and corruption in public office, poor-quality infrastructure, lack of access to good education and healthcare, and inadequate access to schemes. That is why citizens need ways such as grievance redressal, RTI, the media, civil society, writing to representatives and voting to make the government do what it is meant to do.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Evidence: the chapter names problems that remain, such as corruption, poor infrastructure or poor access to education and healthcare
Conclusion: citizens must use ways such as grievance redressal or RTI to make the government act

questions.q: A citizens' group in Guwahati keeps a record of 60 complaints about broken footpaths sent by three routes in one year. 24 were lodged on the state's grievance portal, and 18 of these got an answer within the specified time. 20 were posted on social media, tagging the municipal officials, and 8 got a reply. 16 were letters to local representatives, and 4 got a reply. (a) For each route, what percentage of complaints got an answer? (b) What percentage of all 60 complaints got an answer? (c) Which route did best, and what does the chapter say about this route that explains the result? (d) Name one other way from the chapter that the group did not use. (e) A member says, 'Social media got only 40% replies, so let us stop using it and use only the portal.' Judge this plan.
questions.a: (a) Portal 18/24 = 75%; social media 8/20 = 40%; letters 4/16 = 25%. (b) 18 + 8 + 4 = 30 out of 60 = 50%. (c) The grievance portal: on the Public Grievances Portal and the states' portals, the concerned department responds within a specified time period. (d) Any one: filing an RTI request, engaging through a civil society organisation, voting in elections, approaching a vigilance commission (for corruption). (e) Partly sensible: the portal gave the best rate of answers, so it should stay the main route. But the media also matter: they keep citizens informed and provide a platform for discussion, and 8 complaints were still answered that way, so the group should keep using social media alongside the portal rather than drop it.
s: (c) Portal: the department must respond within a specified time
(d) One other route: RTI, civil society organisation, voting or vigilance commission
(e) Judgement: keep the portal as the main route, but media still help and should not be dropped

questions.q: Ananya's village government school has had no science teacher for six months. Explain how Ananya's family could use four different ways described in the chapter to get the problem addressed, saying in one line what each way would achieve.
questions.a: 1. Grievance redressal: file a complaint with the education department's grievance office or the Public Grievances Portal, which must respond within a specified time. 2. RTI: ask for information on the vacancy and when a teacher will be posted, which brings transparency and accountability. 3. Media: write to a newspaper or post on social media tagging the education officials, so the issue becomes public. 4. Write to the local political representative, or join a civil society group working on education, to press the government to act.
s: A grievance route (office or portal) with what it achieves
RTI request about the vacancy with what it achieves
Media or social media use with what it achieves
Writing to a representative or working through a civil society group, with what it achieves

questions.q: Which part of the government settles disputes and checks whether the laws made by the government are fair and just?
questions.a: The judiciary, which makes sure everyone follows the law, settles disputes and protects people's rights.

questions.q: The chapter says that in India the judiciary is independent. What does this mean?
o: It is not controlled by the government or politicians
Its judges are chosen in every general election
It makes all the laws for the country
It does not have to follow the Constitution
questions.a: It is not controlled by the government or politicians, which helps keep justice fair and equal for all.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Without a strong and fair judiciary, democracy cannot survive. Reason (R): The judiciary keeps a check on unfair actions and ensures that laws do not harm people's rights.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: by checking unfair actions and protecting rights, the judiciary upholds the rule of law on which democracy depends.

questions.q: Name any two functions of the judiciary listed in the chapter.
questions.a: Any two of: protects and defends the laws; interprets the laws; protects the rights and liberty of citizens; safeguards the Constitution through judicial review.
s: First correct function
Second correct function

questions.q: In an inter-school cricket match, the umpire is chosen and paid by one of the two teams. (a) Why might the other team feel the umpire's decisions are unfair? (b) Use this example to explain why the chapter says the judiciary must not be controlled by the government, given that the judiciary acts as a referee when the government or others break the law.
questions.a: (a) The umpire depends on one team, so he may favour it, and his decisions may not be fair to the other side. (b) Through judicial review the judiciary acts as a referee when the government breaks the law; if the government controlled the judiciary, the referee would depend on one side of the dispute. Because it is independent, not controlled by the government or politicians, justice stays fair and equal for all.
s: (a) An umpire who depends on one team may favour it
(b) Judiciary is the referee when government breaks the law; independence keeps justice fair and equal

questions.q: Answer briefly. (a) What is meant by the rule of law? (b) Through what process does the judiciary safeguard the Constitution? (c) Why does the judiciary need to be independent?
questions.a: (a) The idea that everyone must follow the law, even the government. (b) Judicial review, in which it acts as a referee when the government or others break the law. (c) So that it is not controlled by the government or politicians and justice stays fair and equal for all.
s: (a) Everyone, even the government, must follow the law
(b) Judicial review
(c) Not controlled by government or politicians, so justice is fair and equal

questions.q: In one month a district court records 80 cases: 40 in which the police presented a person accused of a crime, 25 disputes between neighbours over land, 10 in which citizens say a government order broke their fundamental rights, and 5 in which two sides disagree about what the words of a rule mean. Ritu says, 'Courts only deal with criminals.' (a) How many of the 80 cases are not about crime, and what fraction of the total is that? (b) Name the function of the judiciary shown by the 10 cases and the one shown by the 5 cases. (c) Is Ritu right? Use the data.
questions.a: (a) 25 + 10 + 5 = 40 cases, which is half (1/2) of the 80. (b) The 10 cases: protecting the rights and liberty of citizens. The 5 cases: interpreting the laws. (c) No. Half the cases have nothing to do with crime: the court also settles disputes, protects people's rights against unfair government action and explains what laws mean.
s: (a) 40 cases, half of the total
(b) Protects rights and liberty; interprets the laws
(c) Ritu is wrong: half the cases are disputes, rights and meaning of laws

questions.q: Two families in a village quarrel over where the boundary between their fields lies. In Village P, the family with more strong men simply moves the boundary stones and the other family must accept it. In Village Q, the matter goes to the district court, which hears both sides and gives a decision that both must follow. Compare the two villages using the chapter's reasons why the judiciary is important: (a) the rule of law, (b) checking unfair actions, (c) people's rights, (d) resolving conflicts peacefully. (e) Then explain why the chapter says that without a strong and fair judiciary democracy cannot survive, using your comparison.
questions.a: (a) In Q everyone, the stronger family too, must follow the law and the court's decision; in P the stronger family acts above any law. (b) In Q the court can check an unfair action such as moving the stones; in P nobody checks it. (c) In Q the weaker family's rights are protected; in P they are lost. (d) In Q the quarrel ends peacefully through a hearing; in P it is settled by strength and may lead to violence. (e) As Village P shows, without a judiciary the stronger side wins and the weaker side's rights are lost. Democracy needs everyone, even the government, to follow the law and needs people's rights protected, and a strong and fair judiciary is what keeps this check.
s: (a) Rule of law: in Q everyone follows the law; in P the strong act above it
(b) Unfair action is checked in Q, not in P
(c) Rights of the weaker family protected in Q, lost in P
(d) Q resolves the conflict peacefully; P by strength
(e) Without a judiciary the strong win and rights are lost; democracy needs the rule of law and protected rights

questions.q: Which of these became the 'third tier' of India's democracy after the Constitution was amended in the early 1990s?
o: Local governments such as panchayats and municipalities
questions.a: Local governments: the panchayati raj system and municipalities, the other two tiers being the union and state governments.

questions.q: According to the chapter, which of these matters is looked after by the Central (Union) Government?
questions.a: Foreign affairs, a matter for the whole country; streetlamps, drainage and parks are handled by local governments.

questions.q: Ravi says, 'Our Block Education Officer runs the whole school system on his own, so everything about our school depends on him.' Which point from the chapter's example of the school education system corrects him?
o: Different levels and parts of government play different, yet interconnected, roles so every child gets the right to education
Schools are managed only by the Union Government in Delhi, and the block officer simply passes on the orders it sends him
Schools are managed only by the courts and the child-rights councils, which protect children's rights and act if they are denied
Each school is managed by its own principal and teachers alone, and no part of the government has any role in running it
questions.a: Schools are not managed by a single person or office: the legislature, the political and permanent executive and the judiciary at different levels play different, yet interconnected, roles to ensure every child gets the right to education.

questions.q: Give any two benefits of decentralisation listed in the chapter.
questions.a: Any two of: stronger local governments; better knowledge of the area by local leaders; more democratic, as people are involved in decisions; local discussion of issues by people who face them; more accountability, as leaders closer to people are easier to question.
s: First correct benefit
Second correct benefit

questions.q: In the chapter's diagram of the school education system, name the part of government that does each action. If it is the executive, say which of its two parts. (i) A new scheme like PM Poshan Yojana is chosen for all government schools of a state. (ii) District and block offices check that every school follows the rules and that teacher training improves.
questions.a: (i) The political executive, the elected ministers who guide policy and make rules, with schemes such as PM Poshan Yojana. (ii) The permanent executive, the non-elected officers such as District and Block Education Officers who ensure laws are followed and improve teacher training.
s: (i) Political executive
(ii) Permanent executive

questions.q: In the chapter's list of tasks, education appears under both the Central Government and the state governments, and land and agriculture appear under both the state and the local governments. What does this tell you about how the three tiers work? Support your answer with an example from the chapter.
questions.a: The tiers are not fully separate boxes: some subjects are shared, and the levels work in different yet interconnected ways. Education, for example, is a concurrent subject: Parliament makes laws such as the Right to Education Act, while states run education in each state through their legislatures, ministers and officers.
s: Some subjects are shared between tiers
The tiers work together in different but connected roles
Example such as education: Parliament's RTE Act and the state running schools

questions.q: The municipal helpline of District A records calls in one month: broken streetlamps 24, blocked drains 18, broken park benches 6, shortage of doctors in the state-run district hospital 12, and questions about a new currency note 2. The municipality fixed 42 of the local-issue calls within a week. In the neighbouring District B, the same kinds of local calls go to an office in the state capital, which fixed 15 of its 50 local calls within a week. (a) Which tier of government should handle each of the five kinds of call in District A? (b) How many of District A's calls are local issues, and what percentage of all its calls is this, to the nearest whole number? (c) What percentage of local calls was fixed within a week in District A and in District B? (d) Which point from the chapter about decisions on local matters do these figures support? (e) An official says, 'District A's figures prove that every matter, including the hospital and the currency, should be left to the municipality.' Judge this using the data and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Streetlamps, drains and parks: local government; hospital doctors (health): state government; currency: Union Government. (b) 24 + 18 + 6 = 48 of 62 calls, 48/62 = 77.4%, about 77%. (c) District A: 42/48 = 87.5%; District B: 15/50 = 30%. (d) Decisions on local matters should be taken at the level closest to the people: the local municipal body can do it faster, and local leaders know the area better than distant officials. (e) Wrong. The figures are only about local issues, where the municipality did better. The 12 hospital calls (health) are for the state government and the 2 currency calls for the Union Government: local problems are solved locally, but bigger issues go to higher-level governments.
s: (a) Correct tier for all five kinds of call
(b) 48 of 62, about 77%
(d) Local matters decided closest to the people: the local body is faster and knows the area
(e) Wrong: data cover local issues only; health and currency belong to higher tiers

questions.q: Imagine two states in the year 1985, before the change of the early 1990s. State X gives its village panchayats funds and the power to decide on wells and village roads. State Y keeps all such decisions with officials in its capital. (a) Why could the two states treat their panchayats so differently at that time? (b) Which state followed more closely the Directive Principle that the state shall organise village panchayats and give them the powers needed to work as units of self-government? Why? (c) Name two benefits of decentralisation that the villagers of State X were more likely to enjoy. (d) After the change of the early 1990s, could State Y still treat local government as something only it decides on? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Originally the Constitution had only two levels of government; local governments such as panchayats were listed under the State List, so each state government could decide how they worked. (b) State X, because it gave its panchayats funds and powers to decide on local matters, so they could work as units of self-government. (c) Any two: stronger local governments; better knowledge (local leaders know the area); more democratic (people more involved in decisions); local discussion of issues; more accountability. (d) No. The Constitution was amended to create the panchayati raj system and municipalities, making local governments the third tier of India's democracy, so they are no longer just a matter on the State List; this was done to strengthen democracy at the grassroots and let people take part directly in decisions.
s: (a) Local governments were under the State List, so states decided how they worked
(b) State X, as it gave panchayats powers to work as units of self-government
(c) Two benefits of decentralisation
(d) No: the amendment made local governments the third tier, to strengthen grassroots democracy
